1a.note: Official key 'false' is WRONG; correct key is TRUE. Sorted ascending array is already a min-heap; Floyd BuildHeap does, per internal node, one child-vs-child comparison (only if a right child exists) plus one parent-vs-smaller-child comparison. For odd n: (n-1)/2 nodes x 2 = n-1. For even n: n/2 internal nodes, but the last one has only a left child (1 comparison), so 2(n/2-1)+1 = n-1. Official claims n for even n by charging 2 comparisons to the one-child node. Simulated BuildHeap comparison counts on sorted arrays for n=2..13: always n-1 (also n-1 for insertion-based build and for merely verifying the heap property). Correct answer: True, n-1 for every n.

1b.note: False. Official counterexample verified: T=10(8(7,.),11), insert 6 -> LL rotation at 8 -> 10(7(6,8),11); delete 6 -> 10(7(.,8),11) != T. Independent brute force over all AVL trees from insertion permutations of 2..7 keys also finds T=2(1,.), x=0 (insert rotates to 1(0,2), delete gives 1(.,2)).

1c.note: False: all keys in 3 home cells gives 3 chains of n/3 (linear search); double hashing (second hash independent of the first) spreads them, load 1/2 gives O(1) expected. Agrees.

1d.note: True (Theta(n)), agree on the key. The keys of the two small halves interleave with the other tree's large half, so the result needs a sorted merge and rebuild (O(n)); lower bound by information (~log C(2n,n) = Omega(n) bits). The official lower-bound sentence 'removing n/2 certainly takes linear time' is hand-waving (cutting a subtree is not linear), so the justification is weak: suggest a הערה that the Omega(n) comes from the interleaving/merge, not from the removal.
1d.ruling: flawed-but-defensible (needs a הערה on the lower-bound argument)

1e.note: False. Simulated BST: 29 is the right child of 6, 29's right child is empty, 48's left child is 6. Official reasoning (48 inserted before 29, so cannot be its child) is valid. Agrees.

2c.note: Re-confirmed: the corrected key FALSE is right. h2 offsets for i=0..6 are 0,6,1,11,10,11,1, only 5 distinct cells, so 6 keys can occupy {0,6,1,11,10} plus one more and a new key with that hash needs more than 7 probes. I re-ran the stored counter-example by hand and by script: hash=k mod 13, inserting 0,13,26,39,52,2 gives cells 0,6,1,11,10,2, i.e. table 0@0, 26@1, 2@2, 13@6, 52@10, 39@11; inserting 65 probes 0,6,1,11,10,11,1 (all occupied) and succeeds first at i=9 (cell 9), attempt 10. Also a brute force over every 6-subset of cells confirms a blocking set exists. 'Constant hash: 7th key needs attempt 11' also verified (cells 0,6,1,11,10 then 9 for the 6th key at attempt 10; 7th reaches cell 7 at i=10). Steps (choice a, 11, 5, 10) agree. This item deviates from the official PDF (which says true) and the same claim in 19B-A 6c is official FALSE, confirming the correction.
